On, the figure is safe but over-buys; off, it is closer to reality but sometimes means buying in a hurry.

Positive increases the asset, negative decreases it. This is the figure that decides whether the note needs approval.
Not every pair is symmetrical: a newer one may replace an older one while the reverse does not hold.
Taken from the fastest supplier declared. Combine it with "what if it is missing" to arrive at a sensible stock level.
Links the stock product to the component tree. That is what makes it possible to ask "which assembly does this spare fit" and the other way round.
Fitting a non-genuine part to a machine still under warranty usually voids the warranty on the WHOLE assembly, not just that part.
Very few pairs are interchangeable unconditionally. Say plainly: for which models only, under what conditions only, and what else has to be done.
Sent %(n)d lines from "%(a)s". The goods sit at the transit location until "%(b)s" confirms receipt.
Received back. The goods go to "Awaiting inspection" — raise an incoming inspection note before returning them to available stock.
A drawing with no revision number cannot be used for ordering — the manufacturer will come straight back and ask.
Many spares are made for the manufacturer by a third party. This code is stamped on the part itself, and usually differs from the OEM code.
The condition on return has to be recorded. Take it back without looking and the next person to borrow it gets a broken one.
Nothing has moved in 12 months. NOT necessarily excess — a spare for a rare failure is supposed to sit still.
Counted from the date the goods were RECEIVED, not the date they were fitted. Sit in store for two years and the warranty expires before it is ever used.
If it arises from a work order, that order has to be named — otherwise the material cost never finds its way back to the order.
Over 90 days. If this kind runs out there is no buying it in time, so it has to be stocked in advance — quite unlike something available within a week.
The consequence of needing it and not having it. This, not the price of the part, is what decides how much to stock.
The person counting and the person approving have to be two different people. Count and approve yourself and the approval step means nothing at all.
Empty means the goods sit in a shared store that every plant can draw on — it is not missing data.
Captured when the note is raised. At approval it is compared against current stock — a difference means the store has moved since.
Gathers the specifications marked "critical" so they are visible on the list itself, before the goods leave the store.
Photographs of the condition, the survey report, the test results. A disposal without evidence is indistinguishable from a loss.
Overdue for return. Without a loan book, tools\n disappear gradually and nobody knows when.
Works certificates, test reports, CO/CQ. Missing paperwork is a discrepancy too — mark it on the matching line.
Overdue. A core returned late is charged for;\n a warranty claim made late is lost.
The planning horizon. Set it at least as long as the longest lead time, or the shortage is discovered when it is already too late to buy.
Returned with a request for recalibration — the tool is locked and cannot be lent out until a new calibration result arrives.
Rotable materials: each serial number is an asset with its own installation and warranty history. The same object, two books recording two sides of it.

Short receipt. The missing part stays at the\n transit location — it has to be found; it does not clear itself.
Note "%s" has been checked and has produced its stock movements — it cannot be cancelled. If the check was wrong, raise a stock adjustment with a reason.
Material bought directly for this job, or supplied by the manufacturer under warranty — it was never in store, so there is nothing to issue.
An emergency issue goes first and the paperwork follows. Until this box is ticked, the request stays on the outstanding list.
Some things are replaced every time (filters, oil); some only when an inspection finds them worn. Put both into the forecast and you over-buy steadily.
An emergency issue still has to declare: %s.\n\nThese are the only three things left to trace it back by, once the goods have left the store with nobody's approval.
A core returned late is charged for; a warranty claim made late is lost. This deadline is the only thing that stops a note being forgotten.
The code has to start with "L" (functional location), "A" (equipment), "K" (bin in a store) or "S" (batch / serial). Received: %s
A specification that, if wrong, means the part does not fit or damages the machine. Shown on the list itself so the storekeeper sees it before the goods go out.
People look for a spare by holding the old one and reading\n                        the number stamped on its casing. That number is rarely\n                        an internal code of ours.
This copy is issued through a work order. A request arising from an incident or a maintenance plan should open a work order first and attach to it.
Line "%s" has rejected goods but no reason. Without one, six months later nobody can answer what exactly this supplier got wrong.
Note "%s" has no deadline. A note with no deadline is a note that gets forgotten — a core returned late is charged for, a warranty claim made late is lost.

%s

Applying the old figures would erase legitimate movements in between. Count again and raise a new note.
Material "%s" is not a stockable type, so there is no stock to reserve. If this is a service or a direct purchase, tick "Not through the store".
This material is not tracked by batch, so no shelf-life warning is possible. Consider setting "Track by batch" and declaring a shelf life on the Stock tab.
The cycle has to be more than 0 months — a cycle of 0 means it is always overdue, and an overdue list that is always full stops being read.
Lines with a discrepancy have to state a reason: %s.\n\nA difference caused by miscounting and a difference caused by a loss look exactly alike unless someone writes down why.
The order that drew this material. It is a real foreign key rather than a note in text, so it can be filtered, counted, and does not break when the order is renumbered.
Goods here are not yet fit to be fitted to a machine: awaiting inspection, quarantined, damaged, or away for repair. This location cannot be chosen as an issuing store.
Many manufacturers sell rotable spares on a core-exchange basis: a lower price, with an undertaking to return the old one within a set period. Return it late and you are charged.

Whether there is any stock at an internal location. Different from "currently installed" — one just removed and not yet back in store is nowhere at all, and that is exactly when it is easiest to lose.
A measuring tool past its calibration date still turns, still clicks, still gives a number — and that number LOOKS right. So an expired calibration bars the loan rather than prompting a reminder.
Note "%s" has no evidence attached. A disposal without evidence is indistinguishable from a loss on the books — and the approver has nothing to look at before deciding.
A discrepancy on %(n)d lines. The rejected goods have gone to Quarantine — they have not been returned to the supplier. Raise a case with the sender before moving them.
Required for rotable materials. The manufacturer only warrants the one carrying that exact serial number — letting the system pick any one in store throws the warranty claim away.
Order "%(lenh)s" still has %(n)d material lines not issued: %(ten)s.\n\nIssue them, or tick "Not through the store" for direct purchases and for goods supplied by the manufacturer under warranty.
Goods away for repair, under warranty claim, or on core return, past the\n               deadline — a core returned late is charged for, a warranty claim\n               made late is lost.
Being removed from a machine does NOT mean it is usable again. Goods needing inspection or already damaged go to a separate location and are not added to available stock until someone confirms it.
%(n)d maintenance schedules fall due but NO plan declares any material.\n\nDeclare materials on the maintenance plans first — without the source data there is no demand to consolidate.

Different from the "component category" (which assembly this spare belongs to). This is whether it is a replacement spare, a consumable, a lubricant or a tool — three things that follow three different stock rules.
The shelf life of a lubricant runs from the date of manufacture, not the date it was received. Sit at the supplier for a year before arriving and the remaining life is far shorter than it appears.
%(sp)s was issued but NO installation period could be opened: under "%(vt)s" there is no functional location of category "%(loai)s". Declare that location, then record the installation by hand.
Tool "%(dc)s" %(ly_do)s — it cannot be lent out.\n\nA measuring tool past its validity still gives a number, and that number looks right. A bolt tightened under torque only snaps months later.

Which store the material comes from. If the crew takes it from the container out on site, choose that store — choose the wrong one and the book is right in total but wrong by place, and nobody finds the goods next time.
Order "%(lenh)s" still declares a return quantity that has not been recorded: %(ten)s.\n\nPress "Record the return" before closing, otherwise those goods are counted as consumed for good.
Requesting material that is already in store — unlike a\n work request (reporting that there is a job to do) and a\n purchase request (asking for money to buy what we do not have).

Goods that left the store before anyone approved it. Each row here is\n               a paperwork debt — the sooner it is closed the better, because\n               whoever remembers the event forgets it too.
Some lines declare a return that has not been recorded. Press\n Record the return — otherwise those goods are counted\n as consumed for good.
Long lead-time order. Run out and there is no\n buying it in time — the stock level has to follow the\n lead time, not the rate of use.
These two are interchangeable is an engineering\n conclusion, not a note. Once declared it waits for approval —\n only once engineering has approved it may one be used for the other.

Material "%s" is tracked by serial number. The exact one to be fitted has to be chosen.\n\nThe manufacturer only warrants the one carrying that serial number — letting the system pick any one throws the warranty claim away.
Moved in two steps through a transit location. Between them the goods are\n in transit — countable, traceable, and the sender's\n responsibility until the receiver signs.

OEM code "%(ma)s" already points to "%(sp)s". An OEM code may point to only one spare part — if the two really are interchangeable, declare that under Equivalent spares rather than duplicating the code.
Rejected goods make a reason mandatory.\n Without one, six months later nobody can answer the\n question "what exactly did this supplier get wrong".
A measuring tool past its calibration date still turns, still clicks, still gives a number — and that number looks right. So an expired calibration bars the loan rather than prompting a reminder.
No rule applying means automatic approval — the value is\n below every threshold. Leaving a request hanging for an approver\n who does not exist is a sure way to jam the store.
In transit. It has left the sending store and not yet arrived at the receiving one — it sits at the transit location and remains the sender's responsibility until the receiver signs.
Approval takes the goods off the books for real, with no way back. Evidence has to be attached — a disposal without evidence is indistinguishable from a loss on the books.

The installation period of "%(ts)s" records an installation date of %(ngay)s — in the future, so it cannot be removed today.\n\nThat record is a PLAN rather than something that has happened. Correct the installation date to match reality, then issue again.
A goods receipt note records how much arrived. This note records what it was like on arrival — complete or short, the right code or the wrong one, intact or dented, with a certificate or without.
Mark as Critical any specification that, if wrong, means the part does not fit or damages the machine — it then appears on the spare parts list itself, before the goods leave the store.
At approval the system reads stock again and compares it with the figure captured at the count. A difference stops it — applying the old figures would erase legitimate movements in between.

It only takes effect for users in the "Stores — only the assigned ones are visible" group. Leave it empty while in that group and NO store is visible — deliberately, so that forgetting to fill it in shows up at once rather than quietly granting a view of everything.
For a site store, choose the plant. LEAVE IT EMPTY for a store shared by every plant — which is the case for the central store holding large spares that move between plants. Empty is not an omission.

Location "%(vt)s" currently holds "%(cu)s". To fit the new one, the one removed has to be declared: fill in "Equipment removed" on the material line.\n\nWithout it a serialised asset is lost track of — and that is exactly what is needed for a warranty claim years later.
Emergency issue — PAPERWORK OUTSTANDING. The goods left the store before anyone approved it. This request stays on the outstanding list until The file has been completed is pressed. Due:

Some material lines have not been taken off stock. Closing the order's file will be blocked until they are issued, or marked Not through the store for direct purchases and for goods supplied by the manufacturer under warranty.

This catalogue answers the question the storekeeper asks before issuing: does this spare fit that machine. Leave the model as free text and "V150-4.2MW" and "V150 4,2 MW" are two different things to a computer.

Users in this group see, and can act on, only the
                stores declared in the "Assigned stores" field.
                Anyone outside the group is unaffected — administration,
                accounting and management still see everything.

Gathers four things of the same shape: a warranty claim, a repair or overhaul, an old core return under a core-exchange agreement, and a wrong-goods return. Every one has a deadline — and the deadline is the only thing that stops a note being forgotten.

Declaring it here is what makes it possible to consolidate spare part demand from the maintenance schedule. Tick replace only when needed for things not changed every time — put them all into the forecast and you over-buy steadily.

Unlike preventive maintenance, which counts running hours. Goods sitting in a store run 0 hours for ever, so they never fall due; while in reality shafts still have to be turned, desiccant replaced, batteries recharged.

Unlike Odoo's own stock adjustment: here a reason is mandatory, approval is required above a value, and both the before and after figures are kept. A difference caused by miscounting and one caused by a loss look exactly alike unless someone writes down why.

Three different things; do not merge them. Slow moving may still be right — a spare for a rare failure is supposed to sit still. Excess is the dead money. Discontinued works the other way round: buy more before it runs out.

Product "%(sp)s" belongs to rotable component category "%(loai)s", so tracking by serial number is MANDATORY.\n\nA rotable material is removed and refitted. Without a serial number, after the second overhaul nobody knows which one is where — and the manufacturer warrants the one carrying that serial number, not "a %(loai)s".

It only takes effect for users in the Stores — only the assigned ones are visible group. Leave it empty while in that group and no store is visible — deliberately, so that forgetting to fill it in shows up at once rather than quietly granting a view of everything.

The goods are sitting in Awaiting inspection and are not counted in available stock. Once confirmed, what is accepted goes to its bin and what is rejected goes to Quarantine — not straight back to the supplier, because a return is a document of its own.

Three different figures. Requested is what was asked for and what gets reserved; Issued is what the store handed out; Returned is what came back. Used = Issued − Returned, and that is the figure that is charged.
Returned goods do not go straight into available stock unless "Still good" is chosen. Being removed from a machine does not mean it is usable again.
